1) we developed a distributed principal component analysis (PCA) algorithm for data that are randomly distributed among the nodes of a network; 2) we developed a novel algorithm for distributed PCA on the sphere, with applications in astronomy; 3) we developed a new distributed algorithm for the leading eigenvector problem, with applications in wireless sensor networks.

we have developed the first distributed algorithms for the problem of principal component estimation and leading eigenvectors on the sphere, with a provable performance guarantee, when the data is distributed among a set computational nodes.

we have developed a distributed principal component analysis method with limited communication, that we have implemented this method in a distributed computing system, and that the method is efficient and accurate in practice.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a novel distributed algorithm for principal component analysis and the leading eigenvector on the sphere with limited communication.
we have designed a novel distributed algorithm for PCA that achieves a linear speedup in the number of nodes, and a linear speedup with respect to the dimension of the data.

we propose and analyze a new distributed algorithm for the problem of principal component computation, which achieves the same convergence rate as the centralized algorithm, while communicating only $O(1)$ bits in each iteration.
The main takeaway from our work is that

when data are distributed among $m$ nodes, it suffices to perform $O(\log m)$ rounds of communication to compute the principal component direction with a relative error $\epsilon$ and $O(\log^2 m)$ rounds of communications to compute the leading eigenvector of the data covariance matrix with a relative error of $\epsilon$.
the problem is surprisingly simple and can be solved in a distributed fashion with very limited communication between the nodes.

, when the nodes communicate in a pairwise fashion and the communication cost is a bottleneck, then the communication complexity of our algorithms is essentially independent of the data dimensionality and is only a function of the desired accuracy of the computed solution and the number of nodes.
